newsitem.title: USA: As G7 host, U.S. has platform to boast on economy.
newsitem.headline: As G7 host, U.S. has platform to boast on economy.

text.p: As it prepares to host the Denver G7 summit, the United States' biggest challenge may be to keep from boasting about its economy, which is blessed with solid growth, low unemployment and a shrinking budget deficit.

Briefing reporters ahead of the June 20-22 summit, U.S. officials have been only too happy to point out the seachange since President Bill Clinton's first summit in Tokyo in 1993, when he was criticised for the swollen U.S. budget defict.

"(In 1993) our partners warned that chronic, growing deficits would inevitably lead to higher interest rates and a drag on world economic growth," Dan Tarullo, the senior White House aide on international economic policy, told reporters.

"In Denver, as in Tokyo, the American economy will be subject to much attention, but this year that attention will derive from the strength of its performance, rather than the risks it could pose to the world economy," he added.

How to sustain global economic growth will be one of the key topics at the summit, which will gather leaders from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. Russian President Boris Yeltsin will take part in all of the Denver sessions except one focusing on economic issues.
At Denver, U.S. officials said they will argue for efforts to promote domestic demand in Japan as well as for structural reforms to boost growth in continental Europe.

According to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the United States is expected to have 3.6 percent growth this year, combined with 5.0 percent unemployment and a budget deficit of only 1.1 percent of gross domestic product.

In contrast, the OECD forecasts France, Germany and Italy to have double-digit unemployment and identical budget-defict to GDP ratios of 3.2 percent this year. Italy's growth is forecast at an anaemic 1.0 percent, Germany's at 2.2 percent and France's at 2.5 percent for the year.

"We have an interest in our partners achieving their own patterns of sustained growth," Tarullo said, saying the United States in particular wanted to see Japanese deregulation and a strong, domestic-demand led recovery in its economy.
"Similarly, we have a strong interest in seeing European economies make the kinds of structural changes that lead to lower unemployment and sustained growth," he added.
Europe is itself engaged in a debate over how to generate more jobs and stronger growth while meeting the tight economic criteria laid down for its achievement of a single currency.

France and Germany are divided over Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in Europe, with France's newly elected socialist government reluctant to commit itself to further austerity in order to meet the economic criteria for a single currency.

The Europeans may be able to bridge their differences over EMU at a European Union summit in Amsterdam this Monday and Tuesday, but if they do not, the matter seems likely to come up on the sidelines of the Denver meeting.
